# Smallpox vaccination with cowpox (`smallpox_vaccination`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/medicine.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Medicine & hygiene (`medicine`)
- Deps: helped by variolation, contagion_theory, controlled_trial
- Core idea: Exposure to a related orthopoxvirus can train the immune system to recognise smallpox without causing smallpox itself. Jenner used material associated with cowpox; later campaigns used vaccinia. Early programmes relayed vaccine from person to person because activity could be lost during a long journey. That practice could also transmit unrelated infections. Local vaccine reactions were expected, protection could wane, and repeat vaccination was used. Reliable vaccine supplies, case finding and vaccination of contacts were central to eradication.
- Pitfalls:
  - Expecting to find cowpox on any farm; it is rare and sporadic, and most sores on udders are something else and give no protection
  - Passing syphilis or other disease arm to arm; even apparently healthy donors could carry infection
  - Believing one vaccination protects for life
  - Letting the vaccine die out; without a chain of fresh arms or careful drying it is lost
  - Telling the milkmaid story as Jenner's flash of insight; the observation was country knowledge, and the farmer Benjamin Jesty vaccinated his family in 1774
- History: europe: 1774 – Jesty (Dorset) inoculates his family with cowpox; 1796 Jenner vaccinates James Phipps and tests him with smallpox; 1798 publication; islamic: 1800–1801 – vaccine sent from Vienna via Constantinople and Baghdad towards India; india: 1802 – first vaccinations in Bombay; americas: 1800 – Waterhouse vaccinates in Boston; 1803–1806 the Spanish Balmis expedition carries vaccine arm to arm through orphan boys to Spanish America and the Philippines; china: 1805 – vaccination reaches Macau and Canton; global: 1980 – WHO declares smallpox eradicated; the vaccine strain (vaccinia) turned out to be closer to horsepox than to cowpox
- Read:
  - Edward Jenner, An Inquiry into the Causes and Effects of the Variolae Vaccinae (1798)
  - Donald R. Hopkins, The Greatest Killer: Smallpox in History (2002)
